cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Obligation, rights in rem and liability
cards.front: What is an OBLIGATIO in Roman law?
cards.back:
A legal bond (VINCULUM IURIS) between creditor and debtor that creates a duty to perform.
• Iust Inst 3.13 pr: OBLIGATIO EST IURIS VINCULUM, QUO NECESSITATE ADSTRINGIMUR ALICUIUS SOLVENDAE REI.
• CREDITOR = entitled party (right/claim); DEBITOR = party bound to perform (duty).
• Either side may consist of one person or several.
• Roman OBLIGATIO covers both sides; English "obligation" usually means only the debtor's duty.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Obligation, rights in rem and liability
cards.front: Why is an obligation "relative" (IN PERSONAM), and how does a right in rem differ?
cards.back:
An obligation binds only the particular creditor and debtor; a right in rem is absolute — enforceable against everyone (ERGA OMNES).
• A's claim lies only against B, never against third persons.
• Right in rem is defined by its relation to a specific object, not to a debtor.
• Everyone must respect the holder's access to and use of the asset.
• Only a third party's interference creates an obligation (restitution, damages, enrichment).

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Obligation, rights in rem and liability
cards.front: Example 1: Leo sells Ajax's stallion Hector to Helena (she does not know it is Ajax's). Is the sale valid — and who holds which right?
cards.back:
Sale valid — the vendor's lack of ownership does not affect validity. Helena has a relative right against Leo; Ajax an absolute right.
• Helena's claim to delivery (due 17 January) lies only against Leo; Leo's price claim only against Helena.
• Ajax vindicates Hector from whoever possesses him — Leo, or later Helena — and wins.
• Leo must then compensate Helena; she sues with the ACTIO EMPTI (buyer's action).

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Obligation, rights in rem and liability
cards.front: When does a person have a private-law right (claim) from the Roman perspective?
cards.back:
When it can be enforced by a court action (usually an ACTIO); the wording of the ACTIO fixes the right's scope and content.
• Relative right → ACTIO IN PERSONAM; absolute right → ACTIO IN REM.
• Remedies may bear other names: VINDICATIO, CONDICTIO, INTERDICTUM.
• The PRAETOR issues the catalogue of remedies and grants them in a FORMULA — or denies protection.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Obligation, rights in rem and liability
cards.front: Property link: what is the REI VINDICATIO, and why is it an ACTIO IN REM rather than IN PERSONAM?
cards.back:
The non-possessing owner's action to recover his thing from whoever possesses it — it enforces ownership, a right good against everyone.
• Not tied to a contract partner: Ajax may sue Leo or Helena, whoever holds Hector.
• Contrast ACTIO EMPTI: lies only between buyer and seller (IN PERSONAM).
• Every right in rem has its own ACTIO IN REM; for DOMINIUM it is the REI VINDICATIO.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Obligation, rights in rem and liability
cards.front: Insolvency: why is a right in rem stronger than a contractual claim?
cards.back:
In bankruptcy unsecured claims are all cut by the same quota; a restitution claim based on a right in rem survives in full.
• Bankruptcy assets are usually worth less than the total claims.
• Each creditor bears a quota of the total loss, e.g. one third.
• So a purely contractual claim loses value in insolvency.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Obligation, rights in rem and liability
cards.front: Example 2: Flavius lets Agatha's deposited statue lose its paint in the rain (damage 1.400) and goes bankrupt. What does Agatha get?
cards.back:
The statue back in full (as owner); her 1.400 damages claim only ranks pro rata — at a 20 % quota she receives 280.
• Ownership = right in rem, unaffected by bankruptcy.
• Damages claim = mere obligation, sharing the loss with all other creditors.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Obligation, rights in rem and liability
cards.front: Liability vs obligation — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Liability = having to answer financially (creditor may seize assets); obligation = having to perform: give, do or refrain.
• Historically liability came first; originally seizure reached the person (debt bondage, sale TRANS TIBERIM).
• Liability matters only when the debtor fails to perform or performs defectively.
• Personal liability: all one's assets (the rule); in rem liability: specific assets only, e.g. pledge.
• For delicts modern usage typically speaks of "liability".

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Content and types of obligations
cards.front: DARE, FACERE, PRAESTARE — what possible contents of an obligation do these terms describe?
cards.back:
DARE = to give, FACERE = to do, PRAESTARE = to owe / be liable for / guarantee a result.
• DARE: delivery of a thing (goods or money); in a narrower sense transfer of ownership.
• FACERE: an action, labour or result — e.g. transport services under a contract for work.
• PRAESTARE: e.g. standing surety; also accessory duties such as warranty.
• "Performance" covers positive acts and omissions; proper performance discharges the obligation.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Content and types of obligations
cards.front: Property link: how can a DARE (delivery, DATIO) both discharge and create an obligation?
cards.back:
Handing over a thing usually fulfils a duty — but in real contracts the delivery itself creates the recipient's duty to return.
• Discharge: the seller "gives" the goods, the buyer the money.
• Creation: a MUTUUM arises only once the money has actually been handed over.
• A DARE of something not owed creates the CONDICTIO INDEBITI.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Content and types of obligations
cards.front: What does the modern umbrella term "law of obligations" cover, and what does it exclude?
cards.back:
Obligations arising from the production, distribution and allocation of goods and services.
• Excluded: relative rights mainly about personal or family matters (family law, law of persons).
• Inheritance-law obligations form their own category.
• Marriage is a contract in modern law but not part of "contract law".

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Content and types of obligations
cards.front: Which four types of obligations did Roman jurists distinguish by their legal basis?
cards.back:
Contracts, delicts, quasi-contracts and quasi-delicts.
• Contracts: bilateral transactions; content follows the agreement (LEX CONTRACTUS).
• Delicts: acts forbidden by law → compensation and/or penalty (POENA).
• Quasi-contracts: obligations from lawful acts outside any contract.
• Quasi-delicts: certain praetorian delicts, partly without fault.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Content and types of obligations
cards.front: What is a delict, and which are the three key Roman delicts?
cards.back:
An act forbidden by law; injuring another by an unlawful (usually culpable) act creates an obligation to compensation and/or penalty.
• INIURIA (assault on body or reputation), FURTUM (theft), DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM (damage to property).
• Victim's claim = private law; the state punishing crimes = public law.
• Example 3: Pius smashes Xerxes' goblet → claim for DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM for its value.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Content and types of obligations
cards.front: What are quasi-contracts? Name the most important ones.
cards.back:
Obligations arising from lawful acts outside any contract.
• Most important: NEGOTIORUM GESTIO and the CONDICTIONES for unjustified enrichment.
• Iust Inst 3.27 adds: ending COMMUNIO, guardianship (TUTELA), LEGATUM PER DAMNATIONEM.
• Difference from contract: no agreement of the parties is the source.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Content and types of obligations
cards.front: Examples 4 and 5: Laura has absent Antonius' earthquake-damaged villa repaired (3.000); Daphne pays Agrippa 500 she does not owe. Which obligations?
cards.back:
Both quasi-contracts: Laura–Antonius = NEGOTIORUM GESTIO; Daphne recovers the 500 with the CONDICTIO INDEBITI.
• No contract in either case — lawful acts outside contract.
• NEGOTIORUM GESTIO balances the interests of principal (Antonius) and gestor (Laura).
• Daphne paid believing she owed it — the typical CONDICTIO INDEBITI case.

cards.topic: Ch. I — Introduction: Content and types of obligations
cards.front: What are quasi-delicts, and why do they matter for modern law?
cards.back:
Later-classical/post-classical term for certain praetorian delicts, incl. liability irrespective of fault — forerunners of modern strict liability.
• Occupiers: ACTIO DE DEIECTIS VEL EFFUSIS and ACTIO DE POSITO VEL SUSPENSO (cf § 1318 ABGB).
• NAUTA, CAUPO, STABULARIUS liable without fault for staff's damage or theft.
• Also: IUDEX QUI LITEM SUAM FECIT (malicious perversion of justice).
• Modern strict liability: e.g. motor-vehicle keepers.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Freedom of contract and the Roman typology
cards.front: Legal transaction vs contract — definitions?
cards.back:
Legal transaction: declaration(s) of intent committing to duties or making dispositions; contract: bilateral legal act binding one or both parties to perform.
• Unilateral transactions need no consent: making a will, abandoning property.
• Every contract is a bilateral transaction — it needs the other party's consent.
• Some contracts (SOCIETAS) are multilateral.
• MUTUUM: bilateral transaction, yet only the lender gains a claim.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Freedom of contract and the Roman typology
cards.front: What are private autonomy and freedom of contract?
cards.back:
Private autonomy = shaping one's legal relationships on one's own initiative; its chief expression is freedom of contract.
• Three elements: freedom to contract, to choose one's partner, to determine the content.
• Contract terms bind the parties like a statute: LEX CONTRACTUS.
• ID QUOD ACTUM EST — what was agreed — is basis and yardstick.
• Ambiguities: interpretation, then supplementary interpretation.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Freedom of contract and the Roman typology
cards.front: What limits private autonomy in contracting?
cards.back:
The legal framework: illegality and immorality, intent to be bound, the lawgiver's choice of binding transactions, and factual possibility.
• Unlawful or CONTRA BONOS MORES → invalid (bribe; penalty securing an engagement or marriage).
• IUS COGENS = norms not alterable by legal transaction.
• Jokes and declarations of legally incapable persons do not bind.
• No one can be obliged to the factually impossible.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Freedom of contract and the Roman typology
cards.front: What is a CONTRACTUS in Roman law, and what marks a regulated (nominate) contract?
cards.back:
CONTRACTUS = transaction enforceable independently in court; a regulated contract has a NOMEN, which also names its court claim.
• E.g. sale, lease, interest-free loan, mandate.
• Mostly defined by subject matter: EMPTIO VENDITIO = goods for money.
• STIPULATIO: defined by form (ritual promise), not subject matter.
• Four types by formation: consensual, real, verbal, literal.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Freedom of contract and the Roman typology
cards.front: What are innominate contracts, and how are they protected?
cards.back:
Agreements outside the fixed typology (e.g. barter) — no NOMEN, no specific ACTIO; the praetor protects them by ACTIONES IN FACTUM.
• Barter (goods for goods) fits no recognised category.
• Formula opening with a description of the atypical deal (VERBA PRAESCRIBERE) = ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Freedom of contract and the Roman typology
cards.front: NUDUM PACTUM: not actionable — so what legal effects can a bare pact have?
cards.back:
Two: as basis of a defence (EXCEPTIO PACTI) and as subsidiary agreement (PACTUM ADIECTUM) to an actionable contract.
• PACTUM DE NON PETENDO: defendant raises EXCEPTIO PACTI and defeats the claim.
• PACTA ADIECTA are enforced by the main contract's regular action.
• E.g. PACTUM DISPLICENTIAE: buyer may test goods and rescind if he dislikes them.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Freedom of contract and the Roman typology
cards.front: PACTA SUNT SERVANDA: what does it mean, and does it apply in Roman law?
cards.back:
"Agreements must be kept" (from canon law) — modern principle overcoming the Roman typology; Roman law decided binding force by contract type.
• Modern: every serious, lawful, possible agreement binds (cf §§ 879, 883 ABGB).
• Roman: PACTA unenforceable; the STIPULATIO was the flexible, content-neutral exception.
• Modern law still asks for a CAUSA — relativising PACTA SUNT SERVANDA.
• CAUSA for enforceability, for transfer of ownership, for keeping possession.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: Gai Inst 3.89: which four ways of creating contractual obligations does Gaius distinguish?
cards.back:
AUT ENIM RE CONTRAHITUR AUT VERBIS AUT LITTERIS AUT CONSENSU — real, verbal, literal and consensual contracts.
• Consensual (CONSENSUS on essentials): EMPTIO VENDITIO, LOCATIO CONDUCTIO, MANDATUM, SOCIETAS.
• LOCATIO CONDUCTIO covers lease, contract of employment, contract for work.
• Common ground: every contractual obligation rests on agreement.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: What is a real contract, and which are the four Roman real contracts?
cards.back:
A contract concluded by delivery of property (DATIO) on the basis of a typical purpose agreed by consent (CONVENTIO).
• MUTUUM — interest-free loan for consumption.
• DEPOSITUM — safekeeping; COMMODATUM — gratuitous loan for use.
• PIGNUS — real contract of pledge.
• CONVENTIO alone is not enough: no handover, no real contract.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: Property link: does concluding a sale make the buyer owner?
cards.back:
No — the contract only creates the obligation to transfer; ownership passes by a separate act of fulfilment (conveyance, e.g. TRADITIO).
• Roman law treats obligation and its fulfilment as distinct transactions.
• TRADITIO needs authority to dispose, transfer of possession and a IUSTA CAUSA.
• Example 1: valid sale, but Leo cannot make Helena owner of Ajax's horse (NEMO PLUS IURIS).

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: How is a STIPULATIO concluded, and why is it special among regulated contracts?
cards.back:
Verbal contract: parties meet and exchange formal question and answer — "SPONDESNE?" – "SPONDEO."
• Defined by form, not subject matter → maximum flexibility; key complement to other contracts.
• Classical alternatives: "PROMITTIS?" – "PROMITTO.", "DABIS?" – "DABO."
• Other verbal contracts: DOTIS DICTIO, PROMISSIO OPERARUM (freedman's services to patron).

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: Causal vs abstract stipulation — what is the difference?
cards.back:
A causal stipulation names the CAUSA of the obligation, which the creditor must prove; an abstract one names no CAUSA.
• Causal: e.g. EX EMPTO ties the promise to a specific sale.
• Abstract: may secure an owed price or be a loan — background hidden.
• Fraudulent use of an abstract stipulation is met with the EXCEPTIO DOLI.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: Example 6: "CENTUM EX EMPTO MIHI DARE SPONDESNE?" – "SPONDEO." The promisor had already paid the price. Does the promisee win?
cards.back:
No — the promise is void and the promisee loses.
• EX EMPTO makes it a causal stipulation tied to a sale.
• The creditor must prove a valid CAUSA; the price debt no longer exists.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: Example 7: Julius asks "SPONDESNE CENTUM MIHI DARE?", Helena answers "SPONDEO". What can Julius claim, and how is Helena protected against abuse?
cards.back:
Julius may claim 100 without stating any legal ground (abstract stipulation).
• The 100 might secure a price already owed or be a loan.
• If Julius sues fraudulently (e.g. for payment already made), Helena needs the EXCEPTIO DOLI.
• The EXCEPTIO DOLI brings out the background and defeats the claim.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: Which action lies on a stipulation?
cards.back:
Stipulations give IUDICIA STRICTI IURIS; the action depends on whether a CERTUM or an INCERTUM was promised.
• CERTUM (CERTA PECUNIA or CERTA RES) → CONDICTIO.
• INCERTUM (e.g. a FACERE) → ACTIO EX STIPULATU.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: How is a literal contract created, and what is it used for?
cards.back:
By an entry in the PATER FAMILIAS' ledger (CODEX ACCEPTI ET EXPENSI), mainly to modify an existing obligation.
• E.g. change the nature of a debt or add a further debtor.
• Entry = fictitious payment → ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE (CONDICTIO).
• Few sources; in classical times replaced by the STIPULATIO with written records.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: Example 8: Hermes owes Philemon 8.000 for a donkey, due 5 September, and asks for three months' extension. How can a literal contract help?
cards.back:
Philemon enters in his ledger that he paid 8.000 to Hermes — from 5 December Hermes owes 8.000 as if under a loan.
• The sale debt is turned into a loan-type debt.
• Philemon sues with a CONDICTIO.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA vs IUDICIA STRICTI IURIS — what is the difference?
cards.back:
The judge's latitude: EX BONA FIDE the IUDEX weighs all circumstances; a strict formula lays down a narrower programme.
• Strict: defences count only if pleaded as an EXCEPTIO (e.g. EXCEPTIO DOLI) in the formula.
• Bona fide: IUDEX considers the claimant's fraud of his own motion — no EXCEPTIO needed.
• Most contractual claims carry a BONA FIDES clause; all consensual contracts do.
• Also non-contractual: claims from NEGOTIORUM GESTIO.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Real, consensual, verbal and literal contracts; actions
cards.front: Example 9: Alexander lends Bellona 1.000 for a year, informally waives the debt shortly before maturity, then sues her a week later. Outcome?
cards.back:
Bellona must plead an EXCEPTIO PACTI (DE NON PETENDO); otherwise the IUDEX may not consider the waiver and she loses.
• The loan claim is a IUDICIUM STRICTI IURIS for a fixed sum.
• IUDEX checks only whether she received that sum as a loan.
• In a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM the waiver would count automatically.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Characterisation of contracts and donation
cards.front: What is an OBLIGATIO NATURALIS?
cards.back:
A legal obligation that is not actionable: it can and should be fulfilled, but the creditor cannot sue.
• If paid, the payee may keep what was paid.
• E.g. contract with a slave: valid and performable, but no action against the slave.
• Reason: slaves are not legal persons — being suable is part of legal capacity.
• Also distinguish OBLIGATIO CIVILIS (IUS CIVILE) vs OBLIGATIO HONORARIA (IUS HONORARIUM).

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Characterisation of contracts and donation
cards.front: Unilaterally vs bilaterally obliging contracts — and what is an imperfectly bilaterally obliging contract?
cards.back:
Unilateral: duties on one side only; bilateral: each party is both debtor and creditor; imperfect: the second party is bound only depending on circumstances.
• Unilateral: stipulation of a sum, MUTUUM — still bilateral transactions!
• Imperfect: mandate — agent must act; principal owes only reimbursement of expenses, if any arise.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Characterisation of contracts and donation
cards.front: What is a synallagmatic contract, and how does it relate to a bilaterally obliging one?
cards.back:
A necessarily bilaterally obliging contract: by its nature each party is creditor and debtor — mutual rights and duties (DO UT DES).
• E.g. buyer is debtor of the price and creditor of the goods.
• Every synallagmatic contract is bilaterally obliging, not every bilateral one synallagmatic (mandate).
• Synallagmatic contracts are always non-gratuitous.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Characterisation of contracts and donation
cards.front: When is a transaction gratuitous, when non-gratuitous?
cards.back:
Non-gratuitous (onerous) if counter-performance is promised in exchange; gratuitous if assumed without aiming at a consideration.
• Reimbursement of expenses or damages is no consideration — mandate stays gratuitous.
• A fee for the task = consideration → no longer mandate but contract for work.
• Brokerage: non-gratuitous but not synallagmatic (broker need not act).

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Characterisation of contracts and donation
cards.front: What is DONATIO, and is a promise of a future donation enforceable?
cards.back:
A gratuitous grant of a pecuniary advantage; a promise of future donation is enforceable only in the form of a stipulation.
• Forms: transfer of ownership, assignment of a claim, remission of a debt.
• Otherwise a donation is valid only once executed (gift transferred).
• Modern law: informal gratuity promises non-binding; at most once a deed is drawn up.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Characterisation of contracts and donation
cards.front: Property link: why does it matter that DONATIO is a IUSTA CAUSA?
cards.back:
Something given with ANIMUS DONANDI passes ownership by TRADITIO; if that fails, the donee can still usucapt (IUSTA CAUSA USUCAPIONIS).
• TRADITIO is causal: no valid cause, no ownership.
• If the donor was not owner, USUCAPIO can cure the defect over time.
• Gift between spouses = no valid donation → no IUSTA CAUSA → no ownership.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Characterisation of contracts and donation
cards.front: LEX CINCIA vs the ban on gifts between spouses — what are the consequences of breach?
cards.back:
LEX CINCIA: breach-donation effective, only a stipulated promise is repelled; spouses: the gift is invalid under IUS CIVILE.
• LEX CINCIA (DE DONIS ET MUNERIBUS): no accepting gifts above a certain value; close relatives exempt.
• Defence against the stipulated promise: EXCEPTIO LEGIS CINCIAE.
• DONATIO ANTE NUPTIAS (before, in view of marriage) is not caught by the ban.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Pre-contractual obligations: when can a party be liable before any contract exists?
cards.back:
Serious negotiations create mutual trust; a party causing the other harm through bad faith may be answerable (modern: CULPA IN CONTRAHENDO).
• E.g. arbitrarily breaking off negotiations after signalling genuine interest.
• Recoverable: negotiation expenses — travel costs, consultant's fees.
• Roman rudiments exist in the law of sale.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Initially impossible performance — and negative vs positive interest?
cards.back:
Promise of initially objectively impossible performance creates no contract; a seller who knew or ought to have known may owe damages.
• Negative (reliance) interest: position as if one had not relied on the contract.
• Positive (expectation) interest: needs a valid contract; position as if duly performed.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Closing a contract: what is required, and what does an error do in Roman law?
cards.back:
Mutual agreement aimed at a specific legal transaction, with intent to be bound — explicit or implied from conduct.
• Jest: no intent to be bound.
• Fundamental error (essential feature of subject matter, nature of transaction) → no contract.
• Other errors: contract valid; recipient protected by rules on defective performance.
• Modern law: outward impression decides; contract valid but avoidable.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: What is SOLUTIO, and when may the creditor reject performance?
cards.back:
Fulfilment: debtor performs, creditor accepts — exact performance extinguishes the obligation.
• Non-recurring obligations (deliver goods) vs continuous ones (rent, services).
• Creditor may reject any performance not matching the contract; limit = ban on chicanery.
• May he withhold counter-performance until full performance → contract of simultaneous performance.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: DATIO IN SOLUTUM vs DATIO SOLUTIONIS CAUSA?
cards.back:
IN SOLUTUM: with creditor's consent something else (ALIUD PRO ALIO) is given instead and discharges; SOLUTIONIS CAUSA: given only to be credited against the debt.
• IN SOLUTUM = substitute performance, debt fully discharged.
• SOLUTIONIS CAUSA = modern giving "on account of performance"; only the proceeds count.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Example 10: Ago owes Bellona 1.000 from a sale and offers a vase instead. What if she accepts it as payment — and what if only to sell it?
cards.back:
Accepted as payment: delivery discharges the debt (DATIO IN SOLUTUM). Accepted to sell and credit: vase fetches 800, Ago still owes 200.
• Variant = DATIO SOLUTIONIS CAUSA.
• Consent of the creditor is required for any ALIUD PRO ALIO.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Third parties and performance: SOLUTIONIS CAUSA ADIECTUS, undertaking to perform another's obligation, assumption of debt?
cards.back:
ADIECTUS: third party merely authorised to receive payment; undertaking: agreement with the debtor; assumption: agreement with the creditor.
• ADIECTUS cannot sue the debtor or dispose of the debt.
• Undertaking: internal only — creditor still sues his debtor, who is freed if the third party pays.
• Privative assumption: new debtor replaces old (Roman law: novation).
• Cumulative assumption: both bound; once one pays, the other is freed.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Contractual liability: which degrees of fault does Roman law know?
cards.back:
DOLUS (malicious intent) and CULPA (negligence: CULPA LATA gross, CULPA LEVIS slight).
• DOLUS MALUS = intent to harm; also used as opposite of BONA FIDES.
• CULPA = falling short of the required diligence without intent to harm.
• Liability is IUS DISPOSITIVUM, but liability for DOLUS cannot be excluded.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Property link: CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS — what does it mean for accidental loss under a contract?
cards.back:
The owner bears the risk of accidental destruction (CASUS) — unless the obligation reallocates that risk between the parties.
• Accidental (no one's fault) defective performance usually creates no contractual liability.
• Who bears the loss is a question of risk allocation.
• So it matters who is owner of the thing when the accident happens.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: VIS MAIOR vs CASUS MINOR — and what is CUSTODIA liability?
cards.back:
VIS MAIOR: unforeseeable, uncontrollable events — debtor generally not liable; CASUS MINOR: loss preventable by guarding (CUSTODIA), esp. simple theft.
• VIS MAIOR: earthquakes, robbers, Germans, pirates, natural death of a slave.
• Without a CUSTODIA duty, unguarded loss counts as accident.
• CUSTODIA liability: for theft etc. without proof of breach — in effect strict.
• Gaius and others later reinterpret it as breach of a duty to guard.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Debtor's delay vs creditor's delay (MORA) — and what follows from delay?
cards.back:
Debtor's delay: debtor fails to tender conforming performance when due; creditor's delay: creditor refuses performance offered as agreed.
• Never both for the same duty.
• In culpable debtor's delay he is liable even for accidental destruction or damage.
• Partner may withdraw, normally after a period of grace; fixed-date deals (bridal bouquet) immediately.
• Delay damages owed either way; delay ends with performance or other extinction.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: What is misperformance (positive violation of contractual duties)?
cards.back:
The debtor performs but breaches contractual obligations or a duty of care, thereby injuring the creditor.
• E.g. a haulier carries a column, which breaks through inexpert handling.
• Cf Gaius D 19.2.25.7 (Case 170).

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Warranty for defects as to quality — what are the buyer's remedies?
cards.back:
Fault-independent liability for an inherent physical flaw: redhibition (cancel and reverse) or reduction of the price.
• Flaw = lacks an agreed feature or unfit for its typical purpose.
• Debtor knew of the defect → creditor also recovers consequential losses.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Warranty of title in Roman law: when does the claim arise and what does it give?
cards.back:
Only after eviction — a third party has successfully enforced its right in rem in court; then at least the price back.
• Debtor owes undisturbed enjoyment (UTI FRUI HABERE LICERE), not an unencumbered title.
• Classical jurists: even an unknowing debtor is liable for the interest in performance.
• Debtor who knew of the defect: claim even without prior eviction.
• Lease: release from further rent instalments.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Formation, fulfilment and impairments of performance
cards.front: Property link: in Example 1, when does Helena have a warranty-of-title claim against Leo?
cards.back:
Only once Ajax has evicted her — i.e. successfully vindicated Hector (REI VINDICATIO) in court.
• While she enjoys the horse undisturbed, there is no title problem.
• For sale, the protected position is proprietary possession.
• Late classical: same if she acquires ownership from Ajax on another ground (ALIA CAUSA).

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Termination and obligations outside contract
cards.front: Which are the main ways a contractual relationship ends?
cards.back:
SOLUTIO, CONFUSIO, waiver, COMPENSATIO, novation, delegation.
• After SOLUTIO only warranty and fault-based defect/care claims remain.
• Novation: new obligation replaces and extinguishes the old one.
• Delegation: order to perform within a three-party relationship.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Termination and obligations outside contract
cards.front: CONFUSIO vs CONCURSUS CAUSARUM?
cards.back:
CONFUSIO: creditor and debtor become the same person (e.g. debtor inherits from creditor) — obligation extinguished.
• CONCURSUS CAUSARUM: creditor gets from B, on another obligation, the very performance A owes.
• Once B has performed, he can no longer claim from A.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Termination and obligations outside contract
cards.front: Waiver and extension: how were they made under IUS CIVILE and by the praetor?
cards.back:
IUS CIVILE: a strict obligation is waived only by stipulation (ACCEPTILATIO); praetor: informal PACTUM DE NON PETENDO via EXCEPTIO PACTI.
• ACCEPTILATIO = formal acknowledgement of performance, usable to release debts.
• Extension moves the due date; may also be granted by PACTUM DE NON PETENDO.
• BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM: IUDEX considers waiver/extension under BONA FIDES.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Termination and obligations outside contract
cards.front: COMPENSATIO (set-off): what are its requirements, and how is it raised in court?
cards.back:
Setting one debt off against another between parties with mutual claims of the same kind (e.g. money).
• Further: maturity, connexity (e.g. same obligation), liquidity (counterclaim easily provable).
• BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM: IUDEX sets off of his own accord.
• STRICTI IURIS: an EXCEPTIO DOLI is required.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Termination and obligations outside contract
cards.front: Example 11: Solon, Diana's mandatary, collects 700 for her and spends 120 reimbursable travel costs. What does Diana get?
cards.back:
On set-off Diana's claim against Solon shrinks to 580.
• Mutual money claims of the same kind, arising from the same mandate.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Termination and obligations outside contract
cards.front: When does a condiction (CONDICTIO) lie, and what is "performance"?
cards.back:
Whoever receives performance must return it if no CAUSA justifies keeping it.
• Key case: paying an assumed debt by mistake → CONDICTIO INDEBITI.
• Denied if the payer knew there was no debt.
• Performance = delivery and receipt with conscious cooperation of transferor and acquirer.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Termination and obligations outside contract
cards.front: Property link: A's material becomes B's by ACCESSIO or SPECIFICATIO. What can A do?
cards.back:
Claim compensation — a restitution claim not based on performance, since B gained the asset without CAUSA.
• ACCESSIO: owner of the main thing acquires the attached component.
• SPECIFICATIO: whoever becomes owner of the newly made thing must compensate.
• Remedies: ACTIONES IN FACTUM, or EXCEPTIO DOLI against the owner's REI VINDICATIO.

cards.topic: Ch. II — Contracts: Termination and obligations outside contract
cards.front: NEGOTIORUM GESTIO: what claims arise between principal and unauthorised manager?
cards.back:
No contract: the gestor hands over all benefits; he can claim his costs and damages from the management.
• Principal: ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM DIRECTA; gestor: ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM CONTRARIA.
• Both are BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA.
• Meddling may be disapproved and make the gestor liable for damages.
